intro.headline: One sigil is the whole reactivity system
intro.body:
Aktion has no `useState`, no `ref()`, no store to register and no re-render call. It has one rule: **a name that starts with `$` is reactive**.

Write `$count = 0` and every part of the tree that read `$count` updates the instant you write to it. `let`, `const` and `var` are all allowed in front and all change *nothing* — they are decoration on a naming rule.

This world is about making that state move: click handlers, named actions, inputs that bind themselves without a handler, and where an atom lives when you want two copies instead of one.

objectives: Tell reactive state from a plain binding at a glance
Wire a Button's `onClick` to a state write
Hand a named action to a handler instead of calling it
Bind an input to state without writing a handler
Give a component its own private state

stages.title: One sigil, one rule
stages.goal: Declare reactive state with $name = value — and know why let and const change nothing.

teach.text:
Aktion has exactly one kind of reactive state: `$name = value`. There is nothing to import, nothing to wrap and no setter to remember.

You read and write it with the **same sigil**. `$count` is the value; `$count = 5` is the write. No `.value` unwrapping, no `setCount`.

`let`, `const` and `var` are all accepted in front of a declaration and all change **nothing** — `const $mode = "dark"` is still reactive and still writable. The `$` is the mechanism; the keyword is decoration.

Writes are tracked by path, so `$user.role = "editor"` only re-renders the parts of the tree that actually read `.role`.

code.caption: declare, then read and write under the same name

infographic.title: What the runtime actually sees
rows: Reactive atom — readers re-render on every write
Plain binding — evaluated once, never re-renders

tips: Path-level tracking is an atom-only privilege: it applies to `$name = value`, not to hook setters or resource bags.

tips.text: `count = 0` is not an error. It is a perfectly good plain binding — it simply never updates the UI, and nothing warns you.

challenge.title: Which one is reactive?
challenge.prompt: Four ways a developer might reach for state on their first day. Only one of them is something the UI will re-render for.

options.detail: Valid Aktion — a plain binding. `let` does not make anything reactive.
No wrapper object. Reactivity is a naming rule, not a proxy.

hints: Three of these come from another framework or declare an ordinary value.
Look at the first character of the name, not the keyword in front of it.
stages.explain: The `$` prefix is not a convention that a linter enforces — it is what the planner looks for when it decides which names to track. That is exactly why `let count = 0` is legal and inert while `let $count = 0` is reactive: the keyword is thrown away, the sigil is not. And because reads and writes use the same name, there is no setter to keep in sync and no stale-closure class of bug to reason about.

codex.def: The one reactive atom. The `$` prefix — not `let`/`const`/`var` — is what makes a name reactive; read and write it with the same sigil.

stages.title: Wire the click
stages.goal: Hand a lambda to onClick and write state from inside it.

teach.text:
An event handler is not special machinery. It is an ordinary prop holding an ordinary function. `Button` has `onClick`; give it a lambda and put the write inside.

Inside any imperative body — a lambda, an action, an effect — the **full assignment operator set** is available: `=`, `+=`, `-=`, `*=`, `/=`, `??=`, `++`, `--`. So `$count += 1` and `$count = $count + 1` are the same statement.

Reading the atom back into the tree needs no subscription. `Text(`Count: ${$count}`)` re-renders on every write purely because it mentioned `$count`.

code.caption: the whole counter — six lines, no wiring

parts.text: the label — the one bare argument in a canonical call
wants a callable; lives in the trailing options object
an imperative body, so assignment operators are legal inside
everything non-positional shares that one object

tips: `onClick` is the canonical prop name; the older `action` alias is still accepted.

tips.text: `Button("+1", () => $count += 1)` also works — the second positional slot *is* `onClick`. But `Button("+1", "primary")` drops a string into that same slot: no handler, no variant, no complaint.

challenge.title: Complete the counter
challenge.prompt: Three slots: the label, the handler prop, and the write. Four of the chips are what a React or Vue developer types on reflex — leave those in the bank.

hints: The bare positional argument of a `Button` is its label.
The prop is the DOM event name in camelCase — nothing is renamed.
The write has to name the atom, sigil and all.
stages.explain: A handler is a prop whose value happens to be callable, which is why a lambda, a named action and `() => doTwoThings()` all fit the same slot with no adapter. And because a lambda body is an imperative body, the compound operators are open to you: `$count += 1` compiles to `$count = $count + 1` and notifies every reader of `$count`. `count += 1` would compile fine too — and update nothing, because `count` was never an atom.

codex.def: A prop holding a callable. Any lambda or named action fits; inside the body you may write atoms with =, +=, -=, ??=, ++ and friends.

preview.program:
$count = 0

$app(Card([
  SectionHeader("Counter"),
  Text(`Count: ${$count}`, { variant: "title" }),
  Buttons([
    Button("+1", { onClick: () => $count += 1, variant: "primary" }),
    Button("Reset", { onClick: () => $count = 0, variant: "secondary" })
  ])
]))

stages.title: Name it, don't call it
stages.goal: Declare a camelCase action once and hand it to a handler by name.

teach.text:
A `function` with a camelCase name is an **action**: a callable that does something, with an optional `return`. Case is only a readability convention — what decides its role is where you use it.

There are two ways to use one. As a handler, pass the **name**: `onClick: save`. As an expression, call it: `$greeting = greet("Ada")`.

Actions are where imperative work belongs — several writes at once, and the feedback that goes with them. `$toast.success`, `$toast.error`, `$toast.info` and `$toast.warning` render their own stacked layer, so you never add a toast component to the tree.

Need to pass an argument to a handler? Wrap it in a lambda: `onClick: () => remove(item.id)`.

code.src:
$draft = ""
$saved = ""

function save() {
  $saved = $draft
  $draft = ""
  $toast.success("Draft saved")
}

$app(Card([
  Input("draft", { value: $draft, placeholder: "Write something" }),
  Buttons([Button("Save", { onClick: save, variant: "primary" })])
]))
code.caption: declare once, hand it over by name

columns.title: Called while the tree is built
columns.note: The object literal is evaluated now, so save() runs now and the button receives whatever it returned.

columns.title: Handed over
columns.note: The button holds the function and calls it when the user clicks.

tips: An action may `return` a value, which is what lets you use the same declaration as an expression: `$greeting = greet("Ada")`.
`$toast` is one of exactly five namespaces — `$util`, `$storage`, `$console`, `$toast`, `$dom`.

challenge.title: Which ones actually handle a click?
challenge.prompt: `save` is an action declared above. Switch ON every value that leaves the Button with a working click handler.
challenge.help: Switch ON the ones that work. Leave the rest OFF.

switches.label: onClick: () => { $draft = ""; $toast.info("Cleared") }
switches.detail: a block body with two statements

switches.label: onClick: "save"
switches.detail: the action's name, as a string

hints: Ask of each one: at the moment this object literal is built, what value lands in the slot?
Two of them put something in the slot that cannot be called at all.
`save` is a function. `save()` is whatever `save` gave back.
stages.explain: `onClick` wants a callable, and an object literal is evaluated the moment the tree is built — not when the user clicks. So `save` puts the function in the slot, while `save()` runs the action right there during render and stores its return value, which is usually nothing: the side effect fires at the wrong time *and* the button ends up with no handler. A string and a number are not callable either. Wrapping in a lambda is how you delay a call you need to pass arguments to: `onClick: () => remove(id)`.

codex.def: A camelCase `function name(args) { … }` — a callable effect with an optional return. Pass it to a handler by name (`onClick: save`), or call it as an expression (`$x = greet("Ada")`).

stages.title: Sigil Storm
stages.goal: Sort names by the only thing that decides.

teach.text:
Names fall down the middle, one at a time. Steer each one into the bin it belongs in.

**Left is reactive. Right is inert.** A name is reactive if — and only if — it starts with `$`. `let $draft` goes left. `const rows` goes right. The keyword in front is noise every single time, and that is the whole point of the run.

Eight sorted correctly clears the stage. Three misfiles ends it.
tips: Move the pointer left or right to steer the falling name.

tips.text: `profile.email` and `$profile.email` both appear. Only the second one is an address the runtime can write to.

challenge.title: Reactive left, inert right
challenge.prompt: Steer each falling name into its bin. The `$` prefix is the only thing that decides — `let` and `const` are decoration.
challenge.note: Move the pointer (or drag) to steer the falling name. It lands wherever it crosses the line.
challenge.winNote: Press Check to bank the XP.

fallback.prompt: Which of these declares something the UI will re-render for?

options.detail: `const` does not make it reactive, and neither does anything else here.
There is no store object to write into. State is a name, not a container.

hints: Ignore every keyword. Read the first character of the name itself.
A member chain counts as reactive only when its root is an atom.
stages.explain: Every run of this drills one decision: the sigil, and nothing else. It matters because the failure is silent — `let count = 0` and `let $count = 0` look almost identical in a diff, both validate, and only one of them makes the page move. When a value in Aktion mysteriously refuses to update, the first thing to check is whether it ever carried the `$`.

codex.def: Only a `$`-prefixed name (or a member chain rooted at one) is tracked. `let`/`const`/`var` never affect it — a plain name is a one-shot binding.

stages.title: Bound both ways
stages.goal: Wire an input to state with no handler at all.

teach.text:
Pass a `$variable` as an input's `value` and the runtime wires it **both ways**: typing writes the atom, writing the atom updates the field. No handler, no `e.target.value`, no controlled-component ceremony.

A member chain rooted at an atom behaves the same way, so `value: $profile.email` binds one field of one object — and only the readers of `.email` re-render.

The binding is a consequence of *what you passed*, not of a special prop. Put a plain string in that slot and the field renders it and drops every keystroke.

`onChange(value)` is still there when you need to *do* something as well as store it. It receives the new value directly — already unwrapped — and works alongside a binding or instead of one.

code.caption: not one handler in the file

code2.caption: onChange receives the value, not an event

tips: `Input`, `Select`, `Checkbox`, `Switch`, `Slider`, `MultiSelect`, `CheckBoxGroup`, `DatePicker` and the rest of the form group all bind this way.

tips.text: `value: "ada@example.com"` is a literal, not an address. The field shows it, the user types over it, and nothing is stored.

challenge.title: What makes it two-way?
challenge.prompt: One token in this call is both *read* and *written* by the runtime. Click the marker sitting on it.

points.tip: the field id — a string, and only ever a string
the prop name — a plain literal would fit here too
a member chain rooted at an atom — an address, not a value
fires on every keystroke, but stores nothing by itself

hints: Two-way means the runtime needs somewhere to put what the user typed.
Three of these markers sit on things that would be identical if the field were read-only.
Which token names an address rather than a value?
stages.explain: Binding is not a prop, a directive or a modifier — it is inferred from the argument. When the value in an input slot is an atom, or a member chain rooted at one, the runtime has an address it can write to, so it installs the write for you. Hand it a literal and there is nowhere to put the keystroke. That is also why `onChange` is genuinely optional here: it is a notification, not the storage mechanism, and it hands you the value already unwrapped so there is no `e.target.value` to remember.

codex.def: Passing a `$atom` (or a member chain rooted at one) as an input's `value` wires reads and writes both ways — no handler required. `onChange(value)` is optional and additive.

preview.program:
$profile = { email: "", updates: false }

$app(Card([
  SectionHeader("Notifications"),
  FormControl("Email", Input("email", { value: $profile.email, placeholder: "ada@example.com" })),
  Switch("updates", { label: "Send me product updates", value: $profile.updates }),
  Text($profile.email ? `We will write to ${$profile.email}` : "No address yet", { tone: "muted" })
]))

stages.title: Two counters, two states
stages.goal: Give a component its own private state and prove it by rendering two.

teach.text:
Where you declare an atom decides who shares it.

At the **top level**, `$count = 0` is one atom for the whole program. Every reader and every writer touches the same value.

Inside a **component body**, `$n = 0` is a declaration *per instance*. Two call sites get two independent atoms: the initializer runs once when that instance first mounts, and later re-renders keep whatever has been written since.

Write a `Counter(label)` that holds its own count, then render two of them side by side. If they move together, the atom is in the wrong place.

code.caption: one atom per call site — the shape, not the answer

layers.label: $total = 0
layers.note: top level — one atom, shared by every reader in the program

layers.label: Counter("Left")
layers.note: its own $n, from the same line of source

layers.label: Counter("Right")
layers.note: its own $n — a second instance, a second atom

tips: Always end a component with an explicit `return`. A body that falls through renders nothing, silently.

tips.text: Instance identity comes from the call site. When siblings can reorder, pin it with the universal `{ key: id }` prop — every component call accepts one — so each instance keeps hold of its own atom.

challenge.title: Write it yourself
challenge.prompt: Write a `Counter(label)` component that declares its own count atom, renders the label with the count, and has a `+1` button. Then render **two** of them in a `Row`, all under one `$app(...)`.

mustWhy: Declare the count atom inside the body — `$n = 0`.
A component that never returns renders nothing.
The `+1` button needs an `onClick` that writes the atom.
Render two counters so you can see that they are independent.

hints: The atom goes on the first line of the body, before the `return`.
`$n += 1` inside the lambda is enough — no props, no store, no context.
`$app(Row([Counter("Left"), Counter("Right")]))` — build the component above it.
stages.explain: The rule is *where*, not *how*. The very same statement means two different things depending on its position: at the top level it declares one shared atom, inside a component body it declares one atom per instance. That is why `Counter("Left")` and `Counter("Right")` count separately with no props, no context and no store — and why lifting that one line out to the top level would silently make both buttons drive the same number. Choosing the scope *is* the state-management decision in Aktion; there is no second API for it.

afterCode.caption: two instances, two atoms

codex.def: A `$name = value` inside a component body is private to that instance — two call sites get two independent atoms. The identical line at the top level is one shared atom.

preview.caption: live — press one and watch the other stay put

outro.headline: The page moves now
outro.body: One sigil declares it, a lambda writes it, a bound input keeps it in sync, and where you declare it decides who shares it. That is the entire reactive model — there is no second half waiting for you.
outro.nextHint: Next: components — turning these atoms and actions into pieces you can hand to someone else.
